narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 68.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest influences pushing the model toward predicting failure. You placed in the second decile after your first year and the bottom decile after your third year, far below the average performance of students who were accepted. These low rankings signaled to the model a pattern of academic struggle that strongly suggested difficulty passing the bar.

Your LSAT score was the next most important factor, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 41, your score sits noticeably above the average of accepted students (37.18). This higher score pulled the prediction toward success and helped offset some of the negative academic signals, yet it was not enough to overcome the overall risk picture.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.70, also above the accepted-student average of 3.23, provided another positive signal, but it carried less weight than your class rankings.

Given these results, you should focus on strengthening your academic record and bar-exam readiness. Consider retaking key courses, seeking structured bar-prep support, or improving your class standing in future semesters before reapplying. This targeted improvement can directly address the factors that led to the rejection. (248 words)
